summary: Describes an abstract mechanism for delivering root keys from an EAP server to another network server that needs them to offer services such as re-authentication to an EAP peer. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: After you prove who you are once, a key can be passed to other helpers so you do not have to prove it again at each one. This document describes how to hand that key over safely.

subtitle: How an EAP server hands derived root keys to other servers so a device can re-authenticate quickly after a handover.

tldr.problem: Root keys derived from the EMSK cannot leave the EAP server, yet other network servers need them to offer services such as re-authentication when a device moves between networks. RFC 5295 and RFC 5296 do not say how those keys are delivered.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a Key Distribution Exchange (KDE): a Key Requesting Server sends one request carrying a Key Request Token over a AAA protocol, and the Key Delivering Server answers with a Key Delivery Token holding the root key.
tldr.outcome: It is only a protocol template. It must be instantiated for a specific AAA protocol such as RADIUS or Diameter before it can be implemented.

facts.label: Transport
facts.value: A AAA protocol, e.g. RADIUS or Diameter

today: RFC 5749 is a Proposed Standard and the data here does not list it as obsoleted or updated. It remains an abstract template, so it is not usable until instantiated for a specific AAA protocol.

sections.title: Why Root Keys Need Delivering
sections.content:
The Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) is an authentication framework. A key-generating EAP method derives a Master Session Key (MSK) and an Extended Master Session Key (EMSK). RFC 5295 reserves the EMSK for deriving root keys for specific usages, and the EMSK cannot leave the EAP server.

Using the MSK to set up link security causes performance and security problems when a device moves between networks (a handover). RFC 5296 therefore defines the EAP re-authentication protocol (ERP), which uses keys derived from the EMSK or a domain-specific root key. But neither RFC 5295 nor RFC 5296 says how a root key reaches the server that needs it. This document fills that gap with an abstract delivery mechanism.

It runs over a AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) protocol such as RADIUS or Diameter. The mechanism is a template: it must be instantiated for one of those protocols to fix message formats and encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: The main key stays locked in a safe at the main office. Other offices still need a copy of a smaller key, so this document says how to send one safely.

sections.title: Root Keys and Their Holders
sections.content:
The document names three kinds of root key (RK), all children of the EMSK: the usage-specific root key (USRK), the domain-specific root key (DSRK) and the domain-specific usage-specific root key (DSUSRK, derived from a DSRK). A network server authorized to hold each kind is called a USR-KH, DSR-KH or DSUSR-KH (key holder).

Two roles matter for the exchange. The Key Delivering Server (KDS) holds an EMSK or DSRK and delivers root keys. The Key Requesting Server (KRS) is authorized to request them. A USR-KH, DSR-KH or DSUSR-KH can all act as a KRS, while the EAP server (together with its AAA server) and a DSR-KH can both act as a KDS.
sections.plainLanguage: Some servers hand out keys and some ask for them. Which job a server has depends on which key it needs.

sections.title: The Key Delivery Architecture
sections.content:
An EAP server normally carries out EAP authentications but is not involved in later handovers or re-authentications by the same peer. Other servers, such as AAA servers, provide those services. The first time a peer asks one of them for a service, that server acts as a KRS and requests the root keys it needs. For later requests, and while the root key has not expired, it can reuse the same root keys to derive fresh keying material.

Because the EMSK cannot leave the EAP server, the EAP server derives each root key itself and exports it to a AAA server that distributes it. Together they are called the EAP/AAA server. Root keys derived from other root keys, such as a DSUSRK, are requested from the holder of the parent key. The KRS and KDS must share an interface, and the KRS provides the input data to derive the key, including the Key Derivation Function (KDF) to use. Every KDS is responsible for storing and protecting root keys and for deriving and distributing any child keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The main office makes the keys, and branch offices ask for the one they need. Each office looks after the keys it holds.

sections.title: The Key Distribution Exchange
sections.content:
The key distribution exchange (KDE) is one round trip of two messages between the KRS and the KDS, both carried inside AAA messages. The path between them must be protected by an appropriate AAA transport security mechanism. The KRS sends a KDE-Request carrying a Key Request Token (KRT), and the KDS replies with a KDE-Response carrying a Key Delivery Token (KDT).

  • KRT is (PID, KT, KL): the peer identifier, the key type (such as DSRK, USRK or DSUSRK) and the key label.
  • KDT is (KT, KL, RK, KN_RK, LT_RK): the key type, key label, the root key itself, its key name and its lifetime.

The lifetime of a distributed key MUST NOT be greater than that of its parent key. Encoding of key types and the AAA attributes are left to whoever instantiates the template; key labels and their IANA registry are covered by RFC 5295.
sections.plainLanguage: One note goes out asking for a key, and one note comes back with the key inside. The key stops working before the key it came from does.

sections.title: Scope and Delivery Scenarios
sections.content:
The context of a distributed key is set by the sequence of key types in the key hierarchy. Its scope is set by the sequence of (PID, KT, KL) tuples and the identifier of the KRS. The KDF includes this context and scope, which binds the key to the specific channel.

There are three scenarios, given the three kinds of KRS:

  • The EAP/AAA server delivers a USRK to a USR-KH.
  • The EAP/AAA server delivers a DSRK to a DSR-KH.
  • A DSR-KH delivers keying material to a DSUSR-KH in the same domain.

The third scenario can be combined with the second into one round trip, so a DSUSR-KH's request passes through the DSR-KH to the EAP/AAA server and the answers return the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: A key can come straight from the main office or by way of a regional office. Sometimes both requests travel together in one trip.

sections.title: Use in ERP Bootstrapping
sections.content:
The KDE is used to deliver the root keys needed by the EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP) from RFC 5296. ERP has two forms of bootstrapping.

In implicit bootstrapping, the local ER server (the KRS) requests the DSRK from the home AAA server (the KDS) during the initial EAP exchange. It puts a KDE-Request in the AAA packet that carries the peer's first EAP-Response, using the AAA User-Name attribute as the PID. If the EAP exchange succeeds, the home AAA server puts a KDE-Response in the message carrying the EAP-Success.

In explicit bootstrapping, a peer that does not know the domain sends an EAP-Initiate message with the bootstrapping flag on. The local ER server adds a KDE-Request to the AAA message carrying it, and the home AAA server answers with a KDE-Response in the message carrying the EAP-Finish with the bootstrapping flag set.
sections.plainLanguage: When you arrive somewhere new, the local helper can either ask for your key quietly while you sign in, or you can ask the helper to do it.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
Every KDE attribute in a request or response MUST be integrity-protected and replay-protected by the AAA protocol that carries it. The AAA protocol MUST use a secure key wrap algorithm to protect the root key in a KDE-Response. Other confidential information, such as identifiers when privacy matters, SHOULD be encrypted.

With a AAA proxy between the KRS and KDS, hop-by-hop security associations mean each intermediary can read the key material. Such hop-by-hop security SHOULD be limited to environments where intermediaries are trusted not to abuse it. Otherwise end-to-end protection between KRS and KDS must be added at another layer.

With explicit ERP bootstrapping, the integrity checksum of the EAP-Initiate message gives cryptographic proof of the peer's consent. With implicit bootstrapping there is no such proof: the peer is unaware of the key request, so a KRS may obtain a root key even if the peer does not support ERP.
sections.plainLanguage: The note carrying the key must be sealed and impossible to replay. Helpers in the middle can peek, so only trusted ones should be used.
